boundaries.evidence: The Definition fixes n>=1, so coordinate and Fourier lattice indices are nonempty. It explicitly defines distance to an empty frequency label set as positive infinity, its finite-width parameter neighborhood as empty, and empty-domain supremum norms as zero. Labelwise families over that set are vacuous; positive-measure conclusions need their separate theorem hypotheses.

The Definition gives O_h by the strict inequality distance<h; therefore O_0 is empty, including for nonempty labels. The real-label homological branch is separately stated as a family over labels, rather than holomorphy on O_0.
The Definition is stated for every n>=1, so n=1 (a single angle and action) is included; the quotient torus, the Fourier coefficients and the Diophantine label set are all defined at n=1 as well.
The Definition requires positive action and angle widths and n>=1. Empty label sets have explicit extended-infimum and zero-norm conventions; finite-width parameter domains then have no points.

boundaries.reason: No boundary-value or endpoint statement occurs: the angular variables are read modulo 2pi and the strips are open, so there are no endpoints to treat.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition remarks identify countable choice in the measure frequency-set suppliers; the positive-measure theorem and its consumers explicitly inherit that assumption. Its analytic notation makes no additional simultaneous selection.

boundaries.reason: The item is a Definition, not an equivalence; only the defining readings exist and there is no forward direction to check.
The item is a Definition, not an equivalence; there is no reverse direction to check.

citations.quote:
Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.
Here **real analytic** has the componentwise meaning of
[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: near every real point each real
component is represented by an absolutely convergent power series in the real
coordinates, and the same coefficients define a holomorphic function on a
complex polydisc whose restriction is the given real component. For a
vector-valued map this condition applies to each of its finitely many scalar
components.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and fix $a\in\mathbb C$ and real numbers $w,h>0$. Suppose the closed rectangle

$$R=\{a+x+iy:0\le x\le w,\ 0\le y\le h\}$$

is contained in $U$. Put $b=a+w$, $c=a+w+ih$, and $d=a+ih$. Its **positively oriented boundary** is the closed rectifiable contour

$$\partial R=\ell_{ab}*\ell_{bc}*\ell_{cd}*\ell_{da}$$

using the directed segments and concatenation of [[def-oriented-complex-triangle-and-boundary]] and [[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]]. Then

$$\int_{\partial R}f(z)\,dz=0.$$

For a rectifiable contour $\gamma$,
$$\int_{\gamma^-}f\,dz=-\int_\gamma f\,dz,\qquad \int_{\gamma^-}|f|\,|dz|=\int_\gamma|f|\,|dz|.$$
For composable rectifiable contours $\alpha,\beta$,
$$\int_{\alpha*\beta}f\,dz=\int_\alpha f\,dz+\int_\beta f\,dz,$$
and the analogous additive identity holds for the absolute integral.

Let $\gamma=x+iy:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a rectifiable contour in the sense of [[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]] and let $f=u+iv$ be continuous on its trace, with real and imaginary parts from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Define
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz:=\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)-\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)+i\left(\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)+\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)\right),$$
where the four integrals are the real Riemann–Stieltjes integrals of [[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]. Their existence is proved in [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]. On a singleton parameter interval the integral is $0$.

Let $0\le r<R<S$, let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,S)$, and suppose $M\ge0$ satisfies $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ whenever $|\zeta-a|=R$. If $n\in\mathbb N$ and $|z-a|\le r$, then

$$|f^{(n)}(z)|\le\frac{n!RM}{(R-r)^{n+1}}.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]]. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $g_j:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Suppose the sequence of partial sums of $\sum_{j\ge0}g_j$ converges locally uniformly to $g$. Then $g$ is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$,

$$g^{(k)}=\sum_{j\ge0}g_j^{(k)},$$

where the derivative series converges locally uniformly.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be one-periodic and continuous. Then

$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|\sigma_Nf(x)-f(x)|\longrightarrow0 \qquad (N\to\infty).$$

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. For $x\in A$ and $y\in B$, the **sections** of $f$ are
$$f_x:B\to\mathbb R,\quad f_x(y):=f(x,y),\qquad f^y:A\to\mathbb R,\quad f^y(x):=f(x,y).$$
Their lower and upper section integrals are the everywhere-defined bounded functions
$$\ell_B(x):=\underline{\int_B}f_x,\quad u_B(x):=\overline{\int_B}f_x,\qquad \ell_A(y):=\underline{\int_A}f^y,\quad u_A(y):=\overline{\int_A}f^y,$$
using [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]. They are defined even when the corresponding section is not Riemann integrable, and always satisfy $\ell_B\le u_B$ and $\ell_A\le u_A$.

If every $f_x$ is integrable and the function $x\mapsto\int_B f_x$ is integrable on $A$, define the **ordinary iterated integral in the $B$-then-$A$ order** by
$$\int_A\left(\int_B f(x,y)\,dy\right)dx:=\int_A\left(x\mapsto\int_B f_x\right).$$
The other order is defined symmetrically. More generally, if the sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, any bounded function $h:A\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is an **exceptionally completed section-integral function**. Its integral, when it exists, is independent of its values on $N$.

Let now $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Its section at $x\in\mathbb R^p$ is
$$E_x:=\{y\in\mathbb R^q:(x,y)\in E\},\qquad g_x:E_x\to\mathbb R,\quad g_x(y):=g(x,y).$$
Empty sections have integral $0$. For a nonempty Jordan section, $\int_{E_x}g_x$ means the Jordan-set integral of [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]. Section integrals over a Jordan set and their iterated integrals are defined by first choosing factor rectangles with $E\subseteq A\times B$ and applying the preceding conventions to the zero extension of $g$. Independence of those rectangles is proved in [[thm-jordan-fubini-by-sections]].

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $m \ge 1$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}^m$ be a nonempty connected open set,
and let $f : U \to \mathbb{C}$ be holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). If there is a
nonempty open set $W \subseteq U$ such that $f(z) = 0$ for every $z \in W$, then
$f \equiv 0$ on $U$.

This is the several-variable identity theorem at the strength the page supports:
the hypothesis is a nonempty **open** set of zeros. An accumulation point of the
zero set is neither assumed nor sufficient in several variables; the companion
page records that stronger one-variable statement as false here.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

derivations.claim:
Fix all variables except one real angle $\vartheta_j$ and put [F1, F2, F6, given, algebra]
$f_j(z)=g(I,\vartheta_1,\ldots,z,\ldots,\vartheta_n,\nu)e^{-ik_jz}$,
with the absent parameter omitted in the phase-only case. Since $k_j\in\mathbb Z$
and $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic, $f_j$ is periodic and holomorphic for
$|\operatorname{Im}z|<s$. For $0<\delta<s$, shift the integration segment
$[0,2\pi]$ to $[0,2\pi]-i\delta\,\operatorname{sgn}(k_j)$; the rectangle
integral is zero by [F2], and the two vertical integrals cancel by periodicity.
On the shifted segment $|e^{-ik_jz}|=e^{-\delta|k_j|}$, so the $j$th Fourier
integral gains that factor. Applying this in each coordinate, using [F6], gives
$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-\delta|k|_1}$. For $0<\sigma<s$ take
$\delta=s-\sigma$; for $\sigma=s$ the claimed bound is the trivial estimate
$|g_k|\le M$.

The number of signed integer vectors with $|k|_1=m$ is at most $2^n$ times [F8, given, algebra]
the number of nonnegative integer $n$-tuples with sum $m$. Choosing the first
$n-1$ entries, each between $0$ and $m$, gives at most
$2^n(m+1)^{n-1}\le2^{2n-1}m^{n-1}\le4^nm^{n-1}$ vectors. Therefore
$$\sum_ke^{-\sigma|k|_1}=\Bigl(\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\sigma|q|}\Bigr)^n\le C_n\sigma^{-n}.$$
For $p=\tau+n-1\ge0$, comparison on $x\in[m-1,m]$ gives
$m^pe^{-\sigma m}\le\int_{m-1}^m(x+1)^pe^{-\sigma x}\,dx$. Thus
$$\sum_{m\ge1}m^pe^{-\sigma m}\le\sigma^{-(p+1)}\int_0^\infty(y+1)^pe^{-y}\,dy,$$
which is finite and proves the positive-power bound after applying the shell
count. If $\tau\ge n-1$, then $m^{n-1-\tau}\le1$ and
$\sum_{m\ge1}e^{-\sigma m}=1/(e^\sigma-1)\le1/\sigma$; this proves the
negative-power bound.

Products of local power series are local power series and satisfy the [F1, F4, given, algebra]
pointwise product bound. For a uniform limit on the full domain, continuity
passes to the limit and every coordinate slice is a locally uniform limit of
one-variable holomorphic functions; [F4] makes the limit separately
holomorphic and hence holomorphic, while passing to the limit in the pointwise
bound gives norm at most $M$.

For $0<\sigma\le1$ and $2\sigma<s$, the estimate of step 1.1 gives on [step 1.1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]
$S_{s-2\sigma}$
$$|g_k(I,\nu)e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}|\le M e^{-\sigma|k|_1}.$$
The product of one-dimensional geometric sums in [F8] is at most
$C_n\sigma^{-n}$; hence the Fourier series is absolutely and uniformly
convergent on the full stated open product. Its sum is continuous and, by
locally uniform convergence and [F4], holomorphic. For fixed non-angle
variables, its Fourier coefficients are exactly $g_k$, by uniform convergence
and [F6]. The difference from $g$ therefore has zero Fourier coefficients and
vanishes on the real torus by [F5], applied successively in the $n$ angle
coordinates. At each real angle point all real derivatives of this difference
vanish; holomorphicity identifies these with its complex Taylor coefficients,
so its local power series is zero on a complex polydisc. The strip
$S_{s-2\sigma}$ is connected, so [F7] gives equality on the full complex strip.
For joint-parameter data, the Fourier coefficient is holomorphic in $(I,\nu)$:
its Riemann sums are holomorphic and converge uniformly on every compact subset
of $B_r\times O_h(\Omega)$, so [F4] and separate holomorphy apply.

The coordinate Cauchy estimate [F3] on a radius-$\delta$ disc about [step 1.1, F3, given, algebra]
$I_j$ gives the first action-derivative bound, and the same argument on the
angle and parameter coordinates gives the other first-derivative bounds. For a
second derivative in the same coordinate, [F3] with order $2$ gives the factor
$2$; for distinct coordinates, use the iterated Cauchy formula on the product
of their coordinate circles, obtaining $M/(\delta_i\delta_j)$. This yields the
stated action, angle, and mixed estimates on their strict smaller domains.

Let $K\ge0$ and choose the coefficient-shift margin [step 1.1, step 1.2, F8, algebra]
$\delta=s-\sigma/2$, which lies strictly between $0$ and $s$. On
$S_{s-2\sigma}$ each discarded Fourier term is bounded by
$M e^{-3\sigma|k|_1/2}$. For $|k|_1>K$,
$e^{-3\sigma|k|_1/2}\le e^{-\sigma K}e^{-\sigma|k|_1/2}$; summing with [F8]
and step 1.2 gives the stated truncation bound, after absorbing $2^n$ into
$C_n$.

On any compact subset of the smaller open product in clause 1 there are [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, F4, algebra]
positive action, angle, and (in the joint case) parameter margins to the
boundary of the original domain. Apply step 1.1 with a fixed strictly smaller
strip width, then apply the coordinate Cauchy estimates of step 2.2 on those
margins. Each differentiated Fourier term is bounded by a polynomial in
$|k|_1$ times $M e^{-\delta|k|_1}$ for some $\delta>0$ depending on the compact
set. The shell comparison of step 1.2 makes these bounds summable. The
Weierstrass test therefore gives locally uniform convergence of each
termwise-differentiated series, and [F4] identifies those sums with the
corresponding derivatives.

boundaries.evidence: The full lattice Z^n and its nonzero-mode subset are nonempty for n>=1, while an empty finite partial sum contributes zero to the nonnegative series estimated in step 1.2. At K=0, the retained nonzero-mode set is empty, T_0g is the zero Fourier mode, and step 2.3 bounds the remaining nonzero-mode tail. If g=0, step 1.1 makes every coefficient zero and step 2.1 gives the zero Fourier series. The joint-parameter label domain is required nonempty in the Statement.

Step 2.1 handles the zero-mode separately when differentiating/representing, and clause 3's divergent-free sums start at k nonzero; the estimates at sigma=0 are excluded by 0<sigma<=1, which the statement records explicitly.
Step 1.1 covers n=1 (the one-variable contour argument) and the shell count degenerates correctly to 4 m^0; clauses 3-4 are stated for every n>=1.
Steps 1.3 and 3.1 treat tau>=0 including the degenerate exponent tau=0, and step 2.3 the borderline case tau>=n-1 for the sum of |k|^{-tau}; both are stated restrictions, not gaps.
Clauses 1-4 fix the margins by strict inequalities (0<delta<r, 0<sigma<=min(s/2,1)); the endpoint sigma=s is not used anywhere, as step 2.1 records when it shrinks the strip.
The Definition cited declares def-countable-choice; the lemma uses it only through the countable summation conventions already fixed there, as noted in step 1.1's absolute convergence argument.

citations.quote:
Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.
Here **real analytic** has the componentwise meaning of
[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: near every real point each real
component is represented by an absolutely convergent power series in the real
coordinates, and the same coefficients define a holomorphic function on a
complex polydisc whose restriction is the given real component. For a
vector-valued map this condition applies to each of its finitely many scalar
components.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]]. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $g_j:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Suppose the sequence of partial sums of $\sum_{j\ge0}g_j$ converges locally uniformly to $g$. Then $g$ is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$,

$$g^{(k)}=\sum_{j\ge0}g_j^{(k)},$$

where the derivative series converges locally uniformly.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

derivations.claim:
*Small divisors.* In (G), $|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha|k|_1^{-\tau}$ for each [given, F1, algebra]
real label and every nonzero mode. In (T), fix $\nu\in O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$
and a retained mode $0<|k|_1\le K$. There is a real label $\nu_0$ with
$|\nu-\nu_0|_\infty<h$, so
$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha|k|_1^{-\tau}-|k|_1h\ge(\alpha/2)|k|_1^{-\tau},$$
since $h|k|_1^{\tau+1}\le hK^{\tau+1}\le\alpha/2$. No discarded mode is
divided by its divisor.

*Convergence and holomorphy.* Let $0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$. For [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]
each label in (G), and uniformly over those labels by the definition of $N$,
or on the joint domain in (T), [F2] and step 1.1 give
$$\sum_{k\ne0}\left|\frac{v_k}{ik\cdot\nu}e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}\right|\le\frac{N}{\alpha_0}\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^\tau e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le\frac{C_{n,\tau}}{\alpha_0}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}N$$
by [F3]. Thus the series is absolutely and uniformly convergent on the
specified phase strip (jointly in all variables in (T)); it is holomorphic in
the phase variables in (G) and jointly holomorphic in (T), by [F4]. Each term
has zero angular mean, hence $[u]=0$. Taking the appropriate supremum gives
the first bound in clause 2, using $\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm G}$ in (G).

*The equation and angular derivatives.* On every strictly smaller strip, [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]
the differentiated series is locally uniformly convergent by [F2] and [F3].
Termwise differentiation yields
$$\partial_{\vartheta_j}u=\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{v_k k_j}{k\cdot\nu}e^{ik\cdot\vartheta},\qquad \nu\cdot\partial_\vartheta u=\sum_{k\ne0}v_ke^{ik\cdot\vartheta}=v-[v]=v,$$
where the last equality follows from [F2]. The extra factor $|k_j|\le|k|_1$
and the two angle margins in clause 2 give the stated one- and two-angle
bounds using [F3].

*Action derivatives.* By [F2], $v_k$ is holomorphic in the action on $B_r$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]
and $|v_k|\le Ne^{-(s-\rho)|k|_1}$. The coordinate Cauchy estimates of
[[lem-cauchy-fourier-and-lattice-shell-bounds]] clause 2, with action margin
$\delta$, give on $B_{r-\delta}$
$$|\partial_{I_j}v_k|\le\frac{N}{\delta}e^{-(s-\rho)|k|_1},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}v_k|\le\frac{2N}{\delta^2}e^{-(s-\rho)|k|_1}.$$
These estimates are pointwise at every label in (G), uniformly by $N$, and
jointly on the smaller parameter domain in (T). Division by the divisor and
summation using [F3] prove the action and mixed action-angle bounds in clause
2, with the explicit label supremum in (G). The locally uniform convergence
also justifies termwise differentiation.

*Truncation.* In (T), $v_k=0$ for $|k|_1>K$ and the solution coefficient [given, step 2.1, algebra]
is defined to be zero there, so every displayed derivative has support in
$|k|_1\le K$.

*Uniqueness.* For a fixed real label in (G), Fourier coefficients of any [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, algebra]
zero-mean phase-holomorphic solution $w$ obey
$(ik\cdot\nu)w_k=v_k$ for every nonzero mode, so every coefficient agrees with
$u$. In (T), the same comparison applies on the open complex parameter domain.
For retained modes, equality follows from step 1.1. For a discarded mode,
$v_k=0$ and $(k\cdot\nu)w_k=0$; away from the hyperplane $k\cdot\nu=0$,
$w_k=0$, and continuity extends this across that hyperplane because its
complement is dense in each open ball. The zero coefficient vanishes by the
zero-mean condition. Fourier uniqueness from [F2] gives equality on the common
domain in either case.

boundaries.evidence: The case of empty Fourier support is included: in case (T) with v=0 the series for u is empty, u=0 is the unique zero-mean solution, and clauses 1-3 remain true by inspection of step 2.1.
Step 1.1 treats h=0 (case (G)) and the zero coefficient v_0, which is removed by the zero-mean hypothesis; the divisor k.nu is nonzero for every retained k by step 1.1.
The statement is for every n>=1; step 1.1's small-divisor estimate is component-free and covers n=1, and the trimmed Fourier support condition in case (T) is vacuous for the zero mode only.

The degenerate case tau>n-1 is allowed, and the case in which the Fourier support meets only finitely many shells is the truncated case (T), whose divisor bound is proved in step 1.1 with alpha_0=alpha/2.

The domain margins sigma<=min(s/2,1) and delta<r are strict; step 3.2 consumes one angular margin per differentiation and never reaches the boundary of the strip, matching the statement's displayed ranges.
Step 2.1 sums over the countable set Z^n\{0}; the countable-enumeration convention is that of the cited Definition, which declares def-countable-choice, and no further selection is made.

citations.quote:
Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.
Here **real analytic** has the componentwise meaning of
[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: near every real point each real
component is represented by an absolutely convergent power series in the real
coordinates, and the same coefficients define a holomorphic function on a
complex polydisc whose restriction is the given real component. For a
vector-valued map this condition applies to each of its finitely many scalar
components.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

derivations.claim: *Structure of $Q$ and $R$.* $Q$ is defined from the holomorphic functions $P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$ and $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$, which are holomorphic on $B_r\times S_s\times O_h$; hence $Q$ is holomorphic there and affine in $I$. Its Fourier coefficients in $\vartheta$ are those of $P(0,\cdot)$ and $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot)$; the cutoff $R=T_KQ$ is the corresponding finite trigonometric polynomial, again holomorphic and affine in $I$, with $R_0=T_K(P(0,\cdot))$ and $R_j$ the truncated coefficients, so $[R]=[Q]$ and $R-[R]$ is zero-mean. This is clause 2.

*Bounds for $Q$.* By [F2] with radii increasing to $r$, at the centre $I=0$ one has $|P(0,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon$ and $|\partial_{I_j}P(0,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon/r$; hence on $|I|_\infty<r$ $|Q(I,\vartheta,
u)|\le\varepsilon+\sum_{j=1}^n rac{\varepsilon}{r}\,|I_j| \le(n+1)\varepsilon .$

*Taylor remainder.* Fix $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ with $|I|_\infty<2\eta r$. By [F3], $P(I)-Q(I)=\int_0^1\bigl(D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)\bigr)\cdot I\,dt$; for $|J|_\infty\le2\eta r\le r/2$ [F2] with $\delta=r/2$ gives $|D_I^2P(J)|\le2\varepsilon/(r/2)^2=8\varepsilon/r^2$ (maximum over the coordinate second derivatives), so for every $t\in[0,1]$, $|D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)|\le n|tI|_\infty\sup_{|J|_\infty\le2\eta r}|D_I^2P(J)| \le2n\eta r\cdot\frac{8\varepsilon}{r^2}=\frac{16n\eta\varepsilon}{r}.$ Therefore $|P-Q|\le\sup_t|D_IP(tI)-D_IP(0)|_1\,|I|_\infty\le n\cdot16n\eta\varepsilon/r\cdot2\eta r =32n^2\,\eta^2\varepsilon$, which is clause 1 with $C=32n^2$.

*Size bounds for $R$.* By step 1.2 and [F1], each coefficient $q_k$ of $Q$ satisfies $|q_k(I,\nu)|\le|Q|_{r,s,h}e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}$ (the decay of [[lem-cauchy-fourier-and-lattice-shell-bounds]] clause 1 with the margin $\sigma\le s$). Hence, on $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h$, $|R|\le\sum_{|k|_1\le K}|q_k|e^{(s-2\sigma)|k|_1} \le|Q|_{r,s,h}\sum_{|k|_1\le K}e^{-\sigma|k|_1} \le(n+1)\varepsilon\,C_n\sigma^{-n},$ by clause 3 of [[lem-cauchy-fourier-and-lattice-shell-bounds]], which is the first bound of clause 3. For $R_j$: $R_j$ is the cutoff of $\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)$, whose coefficients are bounded by $(\varepsilon/r)e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1}$ by [F2] and the same decay; the identical summation gives $\max_j|R_j|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}\varepsilon/r$. For $\partial_{\vartheta_i}R$: by [F2] with $\delta'=\sigma$ and $\delta=r/2$, $|\partial_{\vartheta_i}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)|\le\varepsilon/\sigma$ and $|\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{I_j}P(0,\cdot,\cdot)|\le4\varepsilon/(r\sigma)$; hence $|\partial_{\vartheta_i}Q|\le\varepsilon/\sigma+n\cdot4\varepsilon/(r\sigma)\cdot r \le(1+4n)\varepsilon/\sigma$ on $B_r\times S_{s-\sigma}\times O_h$, and the cutoff of this (holomorphic, affine-in-$I$) function on the smaller strip is bounded by $C_n\sigma^{-n}\cdot(1+4n)\varepsilon/\sigma$, which is the third bound of clause 3.

*Truncation error.* Applying [F2]'s truncation estimate to $Q$ with $\tau=\sigma\le\min(s/2,1)$ and the bound $|Q|_{r,s,h}\le(n+1)\varepsilon$ of step 1.2 gives $|Q-R|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}(n+1)\varepsilon$, which is clause 4 after enlarging the constant; note $e^{-\sigma K}\le e^{-\sigma K/2}$, so the displayed form with $e^{-\sigma K/2}$ holds as well.

boundaries.evidence: If the perturbation P vanishes then Q=R=0 and every clause holds with epsilon=0; step 1.1's coefficientwise construction covers this case without excluding it.
The truncation K=0 is allowed by the statement: R is then the mean of Q, and step 3.1's estimate with sigma K=0 remains valid under the stated sigma<=min(s/2,1).
n=1 is included; the finite sums over the one-dimensional shells in step 2.2 and the segment argument of step 2.1 are dimension-free.
The degenerate margin cases eta=0 and sigma=0 are excluded by the strict inequalities 0<eta and 0<sigma of the statement, which the proof respects when applying the Cauchy bounds.
The truncation error is estimated with e^{-sigma K/2}, so the endpoint sigma=s of the strip is never needed; step 3.1 records that the bound holds under sigma<=s/2.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used: the Fourier cutoff is a finite coefficientwise operation and the segment argument is a finite-dimensional estimate.
