citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, $\tau>n-1$, $\alpha>0$, and let $\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ be the label set of [[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]. Put $\mu:=\tau+3n+2$. Suppose $0<r\le1$, $s,h>0$, $K\ge1$, $0<\sigma\le1$, $8\sigma<s$, $0<\eta\le1/8$, and

$$h\le\frac{\alpha}{2K^{\tau+1}},\qquad K\sigma\ge1,\qquad \eta\le\sigma .$$

Let $P$ be holomorphic and $2\pi$-periodic in the angles on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real-valued on real points, with $|P|_{r,s,h}\le\varepsilon$. Set

$$E:=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha r\sigma^\mu},\qquad E\le c\eta,$$

where $c=c(n,\tau)>0$ is sufficiently small. All constants $C$ below depend only on $n,\tau$. Define the affine Taylor polynomial $Q$ and $R=T_KQ$ by [[lem-kam-affine-taylor-fourier-truncation]], and put $\widehat R=[R]$, $N=\nu\cdot I$. Let $F$ be the zero-mean solution, with Fourier support $|k|_1\le K$, of

$$\nu\cdot\partial_\vartheta F=R-\widehat R$$

from [[lem-truncated-homological-equation-with-conservative-loss]]. Order phase coordinates as $(I,\vartheta)$, so $X_F=(-F_\vartheta,F_I)$, $\omega=\sum_i d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i$, and $\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta$. Put $W=\operatorname{diag}(r^{-1}I_n,\sigma^{-1}I_n)$. Then:

1. **Generator.** $F$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}$, affine in $I$, and $F_I$ is independent of $I$. It satisfies $\{F,N\}+\widehat R=R$ and
$$r^{-1}|F_\vartheta|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}+\sigma^{-1}|F_I|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1},\qquad |W(DX_F)W^{-1}|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1}.$$
2. **Flow.** For $0\le t\le1$, the flow $\Phi_t$ is defined and holomorphic on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, with
$$\Phi_t:D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\longrightarrow D_{3r/4,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
Here parameters are held fixed; $D\Phi_t$ denotes the derivative in $(I,\vartheta)$. The map is affine in $I$, its angle component is independent of $I$, and it obeys $\Phi_t(I,\vartheta+2\pi k,\nu)=\Phi_t(I,\vartheta,\nu)+(0,2\pi k)$. It is canonical, and real on real points. Uniformly in $t$,
$$|W(\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,\qquad |W(D\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})W^{-1}|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,$$
$$h|W\partial_{\nu_j}\Phi_t|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h/2}\le CE\qquad(1\le j\le n).$$
In addition, the small action domain has the inclusion
$$\Phi_t(D_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h})\subseteq D_{2\eta r,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
3. **Remainder.** For $\Phi=\Phi_1$ and $\chi_t=(1-t)\widehat R+tR$, the identity
$$(N+P)\circ\Phi=N+\widehat R+P_+,\qquad P_+=(P-R)\circ\Phi+\int_0^1\{\chi_t,F\}\circ\Phi_t\,dt$$
holds on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, and on the smaller action domain
$$|P_+|_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h}\le C\bigl[E+\eta^2+\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K/2}\bigr]\varepsilon .$$
4. **Frequency shift.** Write $\widehat R(I,\nu)=a(\nu)+v(\nu)\cdot I$. Then $v$ is holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real on real points, and
$$|v|_{O_h}\le B:=C\frac{\varepsilon}{r}=C\alpha E\sigma^\mu,\qquad |Dv|_{O_{h/2}}\le\frac{2nB}{h}.$$

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Let $n\ge1$, $h>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $v:O_h(\Omega)	o\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic with $|v|_{O_h(\Omega)}\le B$ where
$$B\le rac{h}{16n}.$$
Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness.** For every $
u_+\in O_{h/4}(\Omega)$ there is exactly one $
u\in O_{h/2}(\Omega)$ with
$$
u+v(
u)=
u_+.$$
   The assignment $\phi(
u_+):=
u$ defines a map $\phi:O_{h/4}(\Omega)	o O_{h/2}(\Omega)$ with $|\phi(
u_+)-
u_+|_\infty\le B$ for every $
u_+$.
2. **Holomorphy.** $\phi$ is holomorphic on $O_{h/4}(\Omega)$.
3. **Derivative bounds.** With $D\phi$ the complex Jacobian and the row-sum norm, for every $
u_+\in O_{h/4}(\Omega)$
$$\|D\phi(
u_+)-I_n\|\le rac{16n}{7}\, rac{B}{h},\qquad	ext{equivalently}\qquad h\,\|D\phi(
u_+)-I_n\|\le rac{16n}{7}B.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.
Here **real analytic** has the componentwise meaning of
[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: near every real point each real
component is represented by an absolutely convergent power series in the real
coordinates, and the same coefficients define a holomorphic function on a
complex polydisc whose restriction is the given real component. For a
vector-valued map this condition applies to each of its finitely many scalar
components.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Since $C_*\sqrt{E_0}\le q<1$, induction gives $E_{j+1}/E_j=C_*\sqrt{E_j}\le q$ and $E_j\le q^jE_0$. Thus $\sqrt{E_j}\le c$, $\eta_j\le1/8$, and $\eta_j/\sigma_j\le(\sqrt{E_0}/\sigma_0)(2\sqrt q)^j\le1$. This proves (b) and the assertions about $\eta_j$ in (a). Also induction directly gives $E_j=A^{(3/2)^j}/C_*^2$, so $\log E_j=-(3/2)^j|\log A|-2\log C_*$ because $0<A\le q^2<1$.

The action radii decrease because $\eta_j\le1/8$, and $\sigma_j\le\sigma_0\le1$. Further, $K_j\sigma_j=K_0\sigma_02^j\ge1$ and $h_j\le h_0\le1$. By the geometric series, $\sum_{i<j}\sigma_i=2\sigma_0(1-2^{-j})$, whence $s_j=s_0-16\sigma_0+16\sigma_j$ and $s_j-8\sigma_j=s_0-16\sigma_0+8\sigma_j\ge s_0/2$. Since $\sigma_j\le\sigma_0\le s_0/32\le s_j/8$, all remaining assertions of (a) follow.

The inequality $E_j\le c\eta_j$ gives the first bound in (c). For the other bound, divide by $h_jr_j$: $\varepsilon_j/(h_jr_j)=\alpha E_j\sigma_0^\mu4^{\mu j}2^{-\mu j}/h_0\le(\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le1/D\le c$, using $E_j\le4^{-(\mu+1)j}E_0$ and condition 3. Thus (c) holds at every step.

Since $\mu>\tau+1$, condition 3 yields $h_j\le[\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1})]4^{-\mu j}\le\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1}4^{(\tau+1)j})=\alpha/(2K_j^{\tau+1})$, and $h_{j+1}/h_j=4^{-\mu}\le1/4$. Moreover $E_j/h_{j+1}\le4^\mu(E_0/h_0)4^{-j}$, and hence $B_j/h_{j+1}\le(C4^\mu\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le1/(16n)$ by $D\ge16nC4^\mu$. This proves (d) and (f). In particular [F2] applies on $O_{h_{j+1}}\subseteq O_{h_j/4}$, and its image lies in $O_{h_j/2}$.

Put $a:=|\log A|$ and $b:=n\log(1/\sigma_0)+2\log C_*$. All these quantities are nonnegative. Condition 2 and [F3] give $K_j\sigma_j/2\ge L\,2^j\ge a(3/2)^j+b+nj\log2+1$, using separately $2^j\ge(3/2)^j$, $2^j\ge1$ and $2^j\ge j$. Therefore $\log(\sigma_j^{-n}e^{-K_j\sigma_j/2})\le n\log(1/\sigma_0)+nj\log2-a(3/2)^j-b-nj\log2-1=\log E_j-1$. Exponentiation proves (e).

Since $r_j+\sigma_j\le r_0+\sigma_0$, the first sum in (g) is at most $(r_0+\sigma_0)E_0\sum_j4^{-j}\le4(r_0+\sigma_0)E_0$. Also $\sum_jE_j\le(4/3)E_0\le2E_0$ and $\sum_j2^jE_j\le E_0\sum_j2^{-j}=2E_0$. Step 2.2 gives $\sum_j\varepsilon_j/(r_jh_j)\le(\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0)\sum_j2^{-(\mu+2)j}\le(4/3)\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu/h_0$. These establish (g) without any assumption relating $r_0$ to $\sigma_0$.

The definitions give $\varepsilon_{j+1}/\varepsilon_j=(E_{j+1}/E_j)(r_{j+1}/r_j)(\sigma_{j+1}/\sigma_j)^\mu=C_*\sqrt{E_j}\sqrt{E_j}2^{-\mu}=C_*2^{-\mu}E_j\ge3CE_j$. By (e) and $\eta_j^2=E_j$, the remainder bound of [F1] is at most $3CE_j\varepsilon_j\le\varepsilon_{j+1}$. Retraction only evaluates this holomorphic remainder on its parameter subdomain by step 2.3 and [F2], so it cannot increase its sup-norm. The retained widths are $r_{j+1}=\eta_jr_j$ and $s_{j+1}=s_j-8\sigma_j$.

To check feasibility, choose $K_0=\lceil\max(1,2L)/\sigma_0\rceil$ and $h_0=\min(1,\alpha/(2K_0^{\tau+1}))$. As $E_0\downarrow0$, this cutoff is bounded by a constant times $1+|\log E_0|$, so $2DE_0\sigma_0^\mu K_0^{\tau+1}\to0$. For completeness, with $t=|\log E_0|$, choose an integer $m>\tau+1$; for $t\ge1$, $(1+t)^{\tau+1}\le2^{\tau+1}t^m$, so [F4] implies $e^{-t}(1+t)^{\tau+1}\to0$. Thus for all sufficiently small $E_0$ one has $D E_0\sigma_0^\mu\le1/(2K_0^{\tau+1})$, and, for each fixed $\alpha$, also $D\alpha E_0\sigma_0^\mu\le1$. These are exactly the two inequalities needed for condition 3 with the chosen $h_0$. If $\alpha\le1$, the second follows already from the first since $K_0\ge1$; all thresholds are then independent of $\alpha$. Conditions 1 and 2 hold by further decreasing $E_0$ and by the cutoff choice. This proves simultaneous feasibility and completes the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: The sums in clause (g) include the empty initial sum with value 0 and are stated for all j>=0; step 3.1 evaluates them from the geometric bounds and no empty family is discarded.
The case j=0 (the initial stage) is included in every clause; step 1.1 provides the base of the induction and the displayed sum bounds start at j=0.
The statement holds for every n>=2 and the estimates use n only through explicit constants; nothing in steps 1.1-3.1 is specific to a choice of dimension beyond the hypotheses.

Initial conditions 1-3 permit equality at their listed smallness and cutoff bounds. Proof 2.2-2.4 checks the weak parameter, shift and tail inequalities, including B_j<=h_{j+1}/(16n), rather than the former slower parameter schedule.
At j=0 all initial conditions are used directly. Proof 2.1 gives s_j-8 sigma_j>=s_0/2, and Proof 4.1 chooses the upper endpoint h_0=min(1,alpha/(2K_0^{tau+1})) after verifying its lower endpoint.
The recurrence, cutoff ceiling and frequency width in Proof 4.1 are explicit. Geometric sums and the exponential-dominance supplier verify feasibility without simultaneous arbitrary selections.

Let $n\ge1$, $\tau>n-1$, $\alpha>0$, and let $\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ be the label set of [[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]. Put $\mu:=\tau+3n+2$. Suppose $0<r\le1$, $s,h>0$, $K\ge1$, $0<\sigma\le1$, $8\sigma<s$, $0<\eta\le1/8$, and

$$h\le\frac{\alpha}{2K^{\tau+1}},\qquad K\sigma\ge1,\qquad \eta\le\sigma .$$

Let $P$ be holomorphic and $2\pi$-periodic in the angles on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real-valued on real points, with $|P|_{r,s,h}\le\varepsilon$. Set

$$E:=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha r\sigma^\mu},\qquad E\le c\eta,$$

where $c=c(n,\tau)>0$ is sufficiently small. All constants $C$ below depend only on $n,\tau$. Define the affine Taylor polynomial $Q$ and $R=T_KQ$ by [[lem-kam-affine-taylor-fourier-truncation]], and put $\widehat R=[R]$, $N=\nu\cdot I$. Let $F$ be the zero-mean solution, with Fourier support $|k|_1\le K$, of

$$\nu\cdot\partial_\vartheta F=R-\widehat R$$

from [[lem-truncated-homological-equation-with-conservative-loss]]. Order phase coordinates as $(I,\vartheta)$, so $X_F=(-F_\vartheta,F_I)$, $\omega=\sum_i d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i$, and $\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta$. Put $W=\operatorname{diag}(r^{-1}I_n,\sigma^{-1}I_n)$. Then:

1. **Generator.** $F$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}$, affine in $I$, and $F_I$ is independent of $I$. It satisfies $\{F,N\}+\widehat R=R$ and
$$r^{-1}|F_\vartheta|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}+\sigma^{-1}|F_I|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1},\qquad |W(DX_F)W^{-1}|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1}.$$
2. **Flow.** For $0\le t\le1$, the flow $\Phi_t$ is defined and holomorphic on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, with
$$\Phi_t:D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\longrightarrow D_{3r/4,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
Here parameters are held fixed; $D\Phi_t$ denotes the derivative in $(I,\vartheta)$. The map is affine in $I$, its angle component is independent of $I$, and it obeys $\Phi_t(I,\vartheta+2\pi k,\nu)=\Phi_t(I,\vartheta,\nu)+(0,2\pi k)$. It is canonical, and real on real points. Uniformly in $t$,
$$|W(\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,\qquad |W(D\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})W^{-1}|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,$$
$$h|W\partial_{\nu_j}\Phi_t|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h/2}\le CE\qquad(1\le j\le n).$$
In addition, the small action domain has the inclusion
$$\Phi_t(D_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h})\subseteq D_{2\eta r,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
3. **Remainder.** For $\Phi=\Phi_1$ and $\chi_t=(1-t)\widehat R+tR$, the identity
$$(N+P)\circ\Phi=N+\widehat R+P_+,\qquad P_+=(P-R)\circ\Phi+\int_0^1\{\chi_t,F\}\circ\Phi_t\,dt$$
holds on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, and on the smaller action domain
$$|P_+|_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h}\le C\bigl[E+\eta^2+\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K/2}\bigr]\varepsilon .$$
4. **Frequency shift.** Write $\widehat R(I,\nu)=a(\nu)+v(\nu)\cdot I$. Then $v$ is holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real on real points, and
$$|v|_{O_h}\le B:=C\frac{\varepsilon}{r}=C\alpha E\sigma^\mu,\qquad |Dv|_{O_{h/2}}\le\frac{2nB}{h}.$$

Let $n\ge1$, $h>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $v:O_h(\Omega)	o\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic with $|v|_{O_h(\Omega)}\le B$ where
$$B\le rac{h}{16n}.$$
Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness.** For every $
u_+\in O_{h/4}(\Omega)$ there is exactly one $
u\in O_{h/2}(\Omega)$ with
$$
u+v(
u)=
u_+.$$
   The assignment $\phi(
u_+):=
u$ defines a map $\phi:O_{h/4}(\Omega)	o O_{h/2}(\Omega)$ with $|\phi(
u_+)-
u_+|_\infty\le B$ for every $
u_+$.
2. **Holomorphy.** $\phi$ is holomorphic on $O_{h/4}(\Omega)$.
3. **Derivative bounds.** With $D\phi$ the complex Jacobian and the row-sum norm, for every $

$$\|D\phi(

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]]. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

derivations.claim: *Domain inclusions.* On $D_{j+1}$ the step moves actions by at most $Cr_jE_j$, angles by at most $C\sigma_jE_j$ and parameters by at most $B_j$. Take the step smallness so that $CE_j\le1/8$. Then $r_{j+1}/2+Cr_jE_j\le r_j/16+r_j/8<r_j/2$. The angular loss $s_j-s_{j+1}$ is at least $5\sigma_j$, so $s_{j+1}-8\sigma_{j+1}+C\sigma_jE_j\le s_j-9\sigma_j+\sigma_j/8<s_j-8\sigma_j$. Moreover $h_{j+2}+B_j\le h_{j+1}/4+h_{j+1}/(16n)<h_{j+1}$. These inequalities also put the input to $\phi_j$ in $O_{h_j/4}$ and its image in $O_{h_j/2}$. Thus $T_j(D_{j+1})\subseteq D_j$, and induction defines the extended composition on $D_j$ with image in $D_0$. The exact sequence formula for $s_j$ gives $s_j-8\sigma_j\ge s_0-24\sigma_0\ge s_0/4$, and in fact for the sequence with loss $8\sigma_j$ it gives $s_j-8\sigma_j\ge s_0-16\sigma_0\ge s_0/2$. Hence the common larger angular strip $S_t$, $t:=s_0/4+2\sigma_0$, lies in every $D_j$ at $I=0$. Equivariance and fixed-parameter canonicity follow by composition; real parameters remain real by the stated real one-step construction.

*Phase Jacobians in a fixed weight.* Because the phase Jacobians are upper triangular in $(I,\vartheta)$, conjugating their error matrices from $W_j$ to $W_0$ leaves diagonal blocks unchanged, multiplies the upper right block by $(r_j/\sigma_j)/(r_0/\sigma_0)\le1$, and leaves the lower left block zero. Thus $\|W_0(D_zT_j-I)W_0^{-1}\|\le CE_j$. The parameter block satisfies $\|D\phi_j\|\le1+(16n/7) B_j/h_j$. Their products are bounded by $\exp(C\sum E_j)$ and $\exp((16n/7)\sum B_j/h_j)$ respectively. Here $\sum E_j\le2E_0$ and $\sum B_j/h_j\le2B_0/h_0$, since $B_j/h_j=(B_0/h_0)(E_j/E_0)2^{\mu j}\le(B_0/h_0)4^{-j}$. Decrease the initial smallness so the phase product is at most $2$; the parameter product is already at most $\exp(2/(7\cdot4^\mu))<2$, since $B_0/h_0\le(16n4^\mu)^{-1}$. The chain rule therefore gives $\|W_0D_z\Psi_jW_0^{-1}\|\le2$ and $\|D\chi_j\|\le2$.

*The parameter block of the phase composition.* The single-step phase-parameter block in the fixed weight is bounded by $CE_j2^{-j}/h_j$, because $\|W_0W_j^{-1}\|\le2^{-j}$ and $\|D\phi_j\|\le2$. Expanding the parameter block of the product of block triangular extended Jacobians yields one term for each step, with a phase product on its left and a parameter product on its right. Step 2.1 bounds these products by $2$, so $$\|W_0\partial_\nu\Psi_j\|\le4C\sum_{k<j}E_k2^{-k}/h_k\le A E_0/h_0.$$ The last inequality follows from $E_k/h_k\le(E_0/h_0)4^{-k}$. The same product expansion for $D\chi_j-I$ gives $\|D\chi_j-I\|\le A B_0/h_0$. All bounds hold throughout the respective $D_j$; earlier factors are evaluated at the parameter images established in step 1.1.

*Holomorphic increments.* For $(0,\vartheta,
u)$ with $\vartheta\in S_t$, $
u\in O_{h_{j+2}}(\Lambda)$, the straight segment from this point to $T_j(0,\vartheta,
u)$ lies in $D_j$. For the parameter segment this follows by choosing a label within $h_{j+2}$ of $
u$: its entire segment stays within $h_{j+2}+B_j<h_{j+1}$ of that label. The action and angle segments stay inside their convex domains by step 1.1, with the same stronger margins on $S_t$. Integrating the derivatives of $\Psi_j$ along this segment and using steps 2.1-3.1 gives $$|W_0\Delta_j\Psi|\le2CE_j2^{-j}+A(E_0/h_0)B_j\le A E_j2^{-j}.$$ Indeed $(E_0/h_0)B_j=(B_0/h_0)E_j2^{-\mu j}$ and $B_0/h_0$ is bounded by a dimensional small constant. This estimates both changes of phase and changes of the parameter fed into every earlier factor. Likewise $|\chi_{j+1}-\chi_j|\le2B_j$ on this parameter tube. Cauchy's estimate with angular margin $\sigma_0$ gives the displayed first derivative bound on $S_{s_0/4}$ and, for every multi-index $ eta$, the bound $|W_0\partial_\vartheta^ eta\Delta_j\Psi|\le A eta!\sigma_0^{-| eta|}E_j2^{-j}$.

*Frequency Lipschitz bounds without convexity of the label set.* A holomorphic function $f$ bounded by $M$ on $O_a(\Lambda)$ has $|f(
u)-f(
u')|\le4n(M/a)|
u-
u'|$ for labels $
u,
u'$. If $|
u-
u'|<a/2$, their segment stays within $a/2$ of $
u\in\Lambda$, and Cauchy bounds on coordinate discs of radius $a/2$ give the derivative bound $2nM/a$ there. If their distance is at least $a/2$, use $|f(
u)-f(
u')|\le2M$. Apply this argument to the weighted phase increment of step 4.1 with $a=h_{j+2}$. Since $$E_j2^{-j}/h_{j+2}\le4^{2\mu}(E_0/h_0)4^{-j}2^{-j},$$ it proves clause 3 with a dimensional $C_L$. Apply it also to $\chi_{j+1}-\chi_j$, bounded by $2B_j$ on the same tube. The bound $B_j/h_{j+2}\le4^{2\mu}(B_0/h_0)4^{-j}$ makes its Lipschitz series summable. This argument uses no segment contained in $\Lambda$ and therefore applies to disconnected Diophantine label sets.

*Limits and sizes.* The bounds of step 4.1 are summable for every fixed angular multi-index, uniformly on $\mathcal L$. Their series therefore define $\Psi_\infty$, with uniform convergence of all angular derivatives. For each label, holomorphic convergence on $S_t$ and Cauchy differentiation prove holomorphy and identify these derivative limits with derivatives of $\Psi_\infty$. Summing the component bounds gives clause 4 after enlarging $A$; decreasing the initial smallness gives $nAE_0\le1/2$. The identity phase map has zero parameter derivative, so summing step 5.1 gives clause 3 for the limit. The parameter increments have summable sizes $2B_j$ and summable Lipschitz constants, yielding $\chi_\infty$, its displacement bound and its asserted Lipschitz bound relative to the identity.

*Exact invariance data.* By the stated one-step identity, $H_j\circ T_j=H_{j+1}$. Induction on the extended compositions gives $H_0(\Psi_j(z,
u),\chi_j(
u))=H_j(z,
u)=e_j(
u)+
u\cdot I+P_j(z,
u)$ on $D_j$. The perturbation bound holds there because $D_j\subseteq D_{r_j,s_j,h_j}(\Lambda)$. The parameter coordinate is essential: for a parameter-dependent $H_0$ the Hamiltonian transported by the phase map at stage $j$ is $H_0(\cdot,\chi_j(
u))$. This proves clause 5.

The Statement specifies this case: The empty composition is (Psi_0,chi_0)=(id,id). Phase and parameter increments are subsequently bounded together; a zero shift leaves the parameter block equal to the identity.
The statement holds for every n>=2 and the estimates of steps 2.1-4.1 use sup-norms and row sums that are dimension-free; the domain inclusions use n>=1 only.

The degenerate case E_0 at the boundary of the stated smallness is allowed; the constants c and C are chosen in step 1.1 so that the strict domain inclusions hold with the weak inequalities of the hypotheses.
Step 3.1 sums the increments over all j>=0 and step 4.1 the parameter differences; the limit is taken through the uniform Cauchy criterion, so no endpoint of the index set is skipped.

The Statement specifies this case: The augmented compositions (Psi_j,chi_j) are determined by the unique inverse retractions and flows. Uniform limits of this prescribed sequence do not require selecting maps from nonempty sets.

Use the sequences and hypotheses of [[lem-kam-parameter-sequences-satisfy-all-step-hypotheses]], with $n\ge2$, $\mu=	au+3n+2$, $\sigma_0\le s_0/32$, $h_j=h_04^{-\mu j}$ and $E_j\le E_04^{-(\mu+1)j}$. The step constants may be enlarged and their smallness constant decreased, depending only on $n,	au$. Put $\Lambda:=\Omega_{\alpha,	au}$ and $W_j:=\operatorname{diag}(r_j^{-1}I_n,\sigma_j^{-1}I_n)$.

Let $H_0(z,
u)=e_0(
u)+
u\cdot I+P_0(z,
u)$ be holomorphic and real on real points on $D_{r_0,s_0,h_0}(\Lambda)$, with $|P_0|\le\varepsilon_0$. Suppose at every stage the cited one-step suppliers produce the following data:

1. A canonical, $2\pi$-equivariant holomorphic phase map $\widetilde\Phi_j$ on $D_{r_j/2,s_j-8\sigma_j,h_j}(\Lambda)$ with the weighted estimates of [[lem-kam-generator-flow-and-remainder-bound]], affine in $I$ and with angle component independent of $I$.
2. A frequency shift $v_j$ with $|v_j|\le B_j:=C\varepsilon_j/r_j=C\alpha E_j\sigma_j^\mu$, and its inverse $\phi_j$ supplied by [[lem-frequency-reparametrization-by-contraction]] on $O_{h_j/4}(\Lambda)$, satisfying $\phi_j+v_j\circ\phi_j=\mathrm{id}$, $|\phi_j-\mathrm{id}|\le B_j$ and $\|D\phi_j-I_n\|\le(16n/7)B_j/h_j$.
3. The exact transformed identity
$$H_j(\widetilde\Phi_j(z,\phi_j(
u)),\phi_j(
u))=e_{j+1}(
u)+
u\cdot I+P_{j+1}(z,
u)=:H_{j+1}(z,
u),$$
where $|P_{j+1}|\le\varepsilon_{j+1}$ on $D_{r_{j+1},s_{j+1},h_{j+1}}(\Lambda)$.

Define the **extended** step and composition by
$$T_j(z,
u):=(\widetilde\Phi_j(z,\phi_j(
u)),\phi_j(
u)),\qquad T_0\circ\cdots\circ T_{j-1}(z,
u)=(\Psi_j(z,
u),\chi_j(
u)),$$
with $(\Psi_0,\chi_0)=(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})$. Thus parameter changes in every earlier factor are included. Set
$$D_j:=B_{r_j/2}	imes S_{s_j-8\sigma_j}	imes O_{h_{j+1}}(\Lambda),\qquad \mathcal L:=\{0\}	imes S_{s_0/4}	imes\Lambda.$$
There are constants $A,C_L$ depending only on $n,	au$ such that:

1. $T_j(D_{j+1})\subseteq D_j$; all extended compositions are holomorphic on $D_j$, take values in $D_0$, and are equivariant in the angles. They are canonical in the phase variables for each real parameter. Every $D_j$ contains $\mathcal L$.
2. On $\mathcal L$, $\Psi_j$ converges uniformly, together with every angular derivative, to $\Psi_\infty$, holomorphic in the angles for each label. Writing $\Delta_j\Psi:=\Psi_{j+1}-\Psi_j$, one has
$$|W_0\Delta_j\Psi|\le A E_j2^{-j},\qquad |W_0\partial_{\vartheta_i}\Delta_j\Psi|\le A E_j2^{-j}/\sigma_0.$$
3. For every pair $
u,
u'\in\Lambda$,
$$\sup_{\vartheta\in S_{s_0/4}}|W_0(\Delta_j\Psi(0,\vartheta,
u)-\Delta_j\Psi(0,\vartheta,
u'))|\le C_L(E_0/h_0)2^{-j}|
u-
u'|.$$
Consequently the phase limit has weighted frequency-Lipschitz constant $2C_LE_0/h_0$. In the unweighted norm the corresponding bound is $2C_L(r_0+\sigma_0)E_0/h_0$.
4. Writing $\Psi_\infty(0,\vartheta,
u)=(b(\vartheta,
u),\vartheta+w(\vartheta,
u))$, the bounds are
$$|b|\le Ar_0E_0,\qquad |w|\le A\sigma_0E_0,\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}b|\le Ar_0E_0/\sigma_0,\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}w|\le AE_0.$$
One may impose $nAE_0\le1/2$ by decreasing the initial smallness constant.
5. The parameter maps converge uniformly on $\Lambda$ to $\chi_\infty$, with $|\chi_\infty-\mathrm{id}|\le AB_0$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\chi_\infty-\mathrm{id})\le C_LB_0/h_0$. The exact finite-stage normal form is
$$H_0(\Psi_j(z,
u),\chi_j(
u))=e_j(
u)+
u\cdot I+P_j(z,
u),\qquad |P_j|\le\varepsilon_j\quad	ext{on }D_j.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ (in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with
$q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb R^n$; the coordinate functions
$q^i,p_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
$\partial_{q^1},\dots,\partial_{q^n},\partial_{p_1},\dots,\partial_{p_n}$ is the coordinate frame
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). On a phase domain:

1. the **canonical one-form** is the smooth one-form
   $\lambda_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dq^i\in\Omega^1(U)$;
2. the **standard symplectic two-form** is the smooth two-form
   $\omega_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i\in\Omega^2(U)$
   ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]);
3. the **standard symplectic matrix** is the block matrix
   $$J:=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R),$$
   whose blocks are $n\times n$.

The identity $\omega_U=-d\lambda_U$ holds, because the coordinate formula for the exterior
derivative ([[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]) gives
$d\lambda_U=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i=-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$. When $U$ is an induced chart domain of a
cotangent bundle, the published [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]] identifies
$\lambda_U$ and $\omega_U$ with the tautological one-form and the canonical cotangent two-form in
those coordinates; the present definition is the choice-free local coordinate model that the
canonical-calculus items of this page use.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]]. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho$, let
$f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and separately holomorphic, let $r$
be a polyradius with $r_k<\rho_k$ for every $k<m$, and let
$C_k(t)=a_k+r_k\exp(it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. For each multi-index $\alpha$ set

$$c_\alpha:=\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{C_0}\!\cdots\!\int_{C_{m-1}} f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta_{m-1}\cdots d\zeta_0 ,$$

an iterated integral as in the polydisc Cauchy formula. Then, with
$M=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$,

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k},$$

and for every real $\theta$ with $0<\theta<1$ the series
$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
$\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ with

$$f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\qquad(z\in\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)).$$

Since every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$ lies in $\overline\Delta_{\theta r}(a)$ for some
$\theta<1$, the expansion holds throughout $\Delta_r(a)$.

**The coefficients are asserted here only as those iterated integrals.** That
$c_\alpha$ equals $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ needs termwise differentiation
and is not claimed by this statement.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. **Complex $m$-space** $\mathbb C^m$ is the set of
functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so a point $z$ has coordinates $z_k$ for $k<m$,
indexed from $0$ exactly as $\mathbb R^n$ is in this library. With coordinatewise
addition and multiplication by complex scalars it is a vector space over the
field $\mathbb C$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]),
with the standard basis $e_0,\dots,e_{m-1}$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].

**The coordinate identification.** Writing $z_k=x_k+iy_k$ with $x_k,y_k$ real
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define

$$\Phi:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb R^{2m},\qquad \Phi(z)=(x_0,y_0,x_1,y_1,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1}).$$

The interleaved ordering is the one used throughout this page; the ordering that
groups all real parts before all imaginary parts is a **different** bijection,
and nothing below is stated for it. $\Phi$ is a bijection and is
$\mathbb R$-linear.

**Norms agree.** Put $\lVert z\rVert:=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|z_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since
$|z_k|^2=x_k^2+y_k^2$, this is the Euclidean norm $\lVert\Phi(z)\rVert_2$ of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and it is a norm on
the real vector space underlying $\mathbb C^m$ in the sense of
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. Consequently
$\lVert z-w\rVert=\lVert\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\rVert_2$, so the metric of
$\mathbb C^m$, its balls ([[def-metric-ball]]), its open sets, its convergent
sequences, its Cauchy sequences and its continuous maps are **verbatim** those of
$\mathbb R^{2m}$ under $\Phi$. In particular convergence and continuity are
coordinatewise ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]), $\mathbb C^m$ is complete
([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]), and a subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

**At $m=1$ this is the published plane dictionary.** For $m=1$ the map $\Phi$ is
the bijection of [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]] and every clause
above reduces to a clause recorded there. Openness, connectedness and real total
differentiability on $\mathbb C^m$ are always read through $\Phi$, exactly as
that remark reads them through its own identification.

**What $\Phi$ does not carry.** $\Phi$ respects the additive and the real scalar
structure but not multiplication by $i$ in any way visible to a general
$\mathbb R$-linear map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$: an $\mathbb R$-linear map of
$\mathbb C^m$ need not be $\mathbb C$-linear. That distinction is the whole
content of the criterion the page proves next, and it is why "linear" is always
qualified below.

Fix $n\ge1$, $r,s>0$. Let $g$ be of one of the following two types.

- **Joint-parameter type:** $h>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty,
  $g:B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$.
- **Phase-only type:** $g:B_r\times S_s\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, bounded,
  and $2\pi$-periodic in $\vartheta$. In this case put
  $M:=\sup_{B_r\times S_s}|g|$ and omit the variable $\nu$ and all
  parameter-derivative conclusions below.

In the joint-parameter case put $M:=|g|_{r,s,h}<\infty$. In either case, for
$0<\sigma\le s$ each Fourier coefficient satisfies
$$|g_k(I,\nu)|\le M e^{-(s-\sigma)|k|_1},$$
where $\nu$ is omitted in the phase-only case. For $0<\sigma\le1$ with
$2\sigma<s$, the Fourier series of $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly on
the full open product $B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}$ (and also on
$B_r\times S_{s-2\sigma}\times O_h(\Omega)$ in the joint-parameter case),
and its sum is $g$. Every $g_k$ is holomorphic in its non-angle variables.
The series and every series obtained by differentiating in $I$, $\vartheta$,
or (in the joint-parameter case) $\nu$ converge locally uniformly on the
corresponding open product and may be differentiated termwise there.

For the joint-parameter type, and for all indicated indices,
$$|\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac M\delta\quad(0<\delta<r),\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac M{\delta'}\quad(0<\delta'<s),$$
$$|\partial_{\nu_j}g|_{r,s,h-\delta''}\le\frac M{\delta''}\quad(0<\delta''<h),$$
$$|\partial_{I_i}\partial_{I_j}g|_{r-\delta,s,h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta^2},\qquad |\partial_{\vartheta_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta'^2},\qquad |\partial_{I_i}\partial_{\vartheta_j}g|_{r-\delta,s-\delta',h}\le\frac{2M}{\delta\delta'}.$$
The same action and angle inequalities hold in the phase-only case with all
parameter slots omitted. These estimates are on the stated smaller open domains;
no uniform derivative convergence on the original open domain is asserted.

For every integer $m\ge1$ and $0<\sigma\le1$,
$$\#\{k\in\mathbb Z^n:|k|_1=m\}\le4^n m^{n-1},\qquad \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-n},$$
$$\sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_{n,\tau}\sigma^{-(\tau+n)}\quad(\tau\ge0),\qquad \sum_{k\ne0}|k|_1^{-\tau}e^{-\sigma|k|_1}\le C_n\sigma^{-1}\quad(\tau\ge n-1).$$
Here constants depend only on the displayed subscripts. For $K\ge0$ and
$0<\sigma\le1$ with $2\sigma<s$, the Fourier cutoff satisfies
$$|g-T_Kg|_{r,s-2\sigma,h}\le C_n\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K}M$$
in the joint-parameter case, with the analogous phase-only supremum bound.
Products of bounded holomorphic functions on the same domain are holomorphic
and obey the product sup-norm bound. A uniform limit on the full domain of
holomorphic functions with norms at most $M$ is holomorphic and has norm at
most $M$.

Let $n\ge1$, $\tau>n-1$, $\alpha>0$, and let $\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ be the label set of [[def-holomorphic-kam-domain-and-diophantine-labels]]. Put $\mu:=\tau+3n+2$. Suppose $0<r\le1$, $s,h>0$, $K\ge1$, $0<\sigma\le1$, $8\sigma<s$, $0<\eta\le1/8$, and

$$h\le\frac{\alpha}{2K^{\tau+1}},\qquad K\sigma\ge1,\qquad \eta\le\sigma .$$

Let $P$ be holomorphic and $2\pi$-periodic in the angles on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real-valued on real points, with $|P|_{r,s,h}\le\varepsilon$. Set

$$E:=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha r\sigma^\mu},\qquad E\le c\eta,$$

where $c=c(n,\tau)>0$ is sufficiently small. All constants $C$ below depend only on $n,\tau$. Define the affine Taylor polynomial $Q$ and $R=T_KQ$ by [[lem-kam-affine-taylor-fourier-truncation]], and put $\widehat R=[R]$, $N=\nu\cdot I$. Let $F$ be the zero-mean solution, with Fourier support $|k|_1\le K$, of

$$\nu\cdot\partial_\vartheta F=R-\widehat R$$

from [[lem-truncated-homological-equation-with-conservative-loss]]. Order phase coordinates as $(I,\vartheta)$, so $X_F=(-F_\vartheta,F_I)$, $\omega=\sum_i d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i$, and $\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta$. Put $W=\operatorname{diag}(r^{-1}I_n,\sigma^{-1}I_n)$. Then:

1. **Generator.** $F$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s-2\sigma,h}$, affine in $I$, and $F_I$ is independent of $I$. It satisfies $\{F,N\}+\widehat R=R$ and
$$r^{-1}|F_\vartheta|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}+\sigma^{-1}|F_I|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1},\qquad |W(DX_F)W^{-1}|_{3r/4,s-6\sigma,h}\le CE\sigma^{n+1}.$$
2. **Flow.** For $0\le t\le1$, the flow $\Phi_t$ is defined and holomorphic on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, with
$$\Phi_t:D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\longrightarrow D_{3r/4,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
Here parameters are held fixed; $D\Phi_t$ denotes the derivative in $(I,\vartheta)$. The map is affine in $I$, its angle component is independent of $I$, and it obeys $\Phi_t(I,\vartheta+2\pi k,\nu)=\Phi_t(I,\vartheta,\nu)+(0,2\pi k)$. It is canonical, and real on real points. Uniformly in $t$,
$$|W(\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,\qquad |W(D\Phi_t-\mathrm{id})W^{-1}|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}\le CE,$$
$$h|W\partial_{\nu_j}\Phi_t|_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h/2}\le CE\qquad(1\le j\le n).$$
In addition, the small action domain has the inclusion
$$\Phi_t(D_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h})\subseteq D_{2\eta r,s-7\sigma,h}.$$
3. **Remainder.** For $\Phi=\Phi_1$ and $\chi_t=(1-t)\widehat R+tR$, the identity
$$(N+P)\circ\Phi=N+\widehat R+P_+,\qquad P_+=(P-R)\circ\Phi+\int_0^1\{\chi_t,F\}\circ\Phi_t\,dt$$
holds on $D_{r/2,s-8\sigma,h}$, and on the smaller action domain
$$|P_+|_{\eta r,s-8\sigma,h}\le C\bigl[E+\eta^2+\sigma^{-n}e^{-\sigma K/2}\bigr]\varepsilon .$$
4. **Frequency shift.** Write $\widehat R(I,\nu)=a(\nu)+v(\nu)\cdot I$. Then $v$ is holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$, real on real points, and
$$|v|_{O_h}\le B:=C\frac{\varepsilon}{r}=C\alpha E\sigma^\mu,\qquad |Dv|_{O_{h/2}}\le\frac{2nB}{h}.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and give $\mathbb{R}^n$ the product
topology, which is the metric topology of $d_\infty$
([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]]).
Recall that $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a real vector space under coordinatewise operations
([[def-vector-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

A subset $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is **convex** when

$$x, y \in C \ \text{ and } \ t \in [0,1] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (1-t)x + ty \in C$$

([[def-interval]]). Then:

1. **Every convex $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is path-connected**
   ([[def-path-connected]]), hence connected ([[def-connected-space]],
   [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]).
2. **Every ball is convex**, in each of the norms $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$,
   $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$
   ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[def-metric-ball]]); so every ball of
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ is path-connected and connected.
3. **$\mathbb{R}^n$ itself is convex**, hence path-connected and connected, and
   so is every half-space
   $\{\, x : x_k \le c \,\}$, and every box $\prod_{k<n} J_k$ with each $J_k$ an
   order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $X$ be a topological space, with subsets carrying the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **The unit interval is connected.** $I = [0,1]$ is a connected subset of
   $\mathbb{R}$, hence a connected space.
2. **Path-connected implies connected.** If $X$ is path-connected
   ([[def-path-connected]]) then $X$ is connected ([[def-connected-space]]). The
   same holds for a subset: a path-connected subset of $X$ is a connected subset
   of $X$.
3. **Path components refine components.** For every $x \in X$,
   $$P(x) \;\subseteq\; C(x),$$
   the path component inside the component
   ([[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]). So every component is a
   union of path components.

**No converse is claimed.** Claim 2 is one-directional and claim 3 is an
inclusion; the question of when a connected space is path-connected is not
settled here.

**No choice principle is used.** The proof takes the union over the **set of all**
paths issuing from a fixed point rather than selecting one path per endpoint,
which is what an appeal to the Axiom of Choice would be. The point at which the
temptation arises is flagged in the remarks.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. **Complex $m$-space** $\mathbb C^m$ is the set of
functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so a point $z$ has coordinates $z_k$ for $k<m$,
indexed from $0$ exactly as $\mathbb R^n$ is in this library. With coordinatewise
addition and multiplication by complex scalars it is a vector space over the
field $\mathbb C$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]),
with the standard basis $e_0,\dots,e_{m-1}$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].

**The coordinate identification.** Writing $z_k=x_k+iy_k$ with $x_k,y_k$ real
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define

$$\Phi:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb R^{2m},\qquad \Phi(z)=(x_0,y_0,x_1,y_1,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1}).$$

The interleaved ordering is the one used throughout this page; the ordering that
groups all real parts before all imaginary parts is a **different** bijection,
and nothing below is stated for it. $\Phi$ is a bijection and is
$\mathbb R$-linear.

**Norms agree.** Put $\lVert z\rVert:=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|z_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since
$|z_k|^2=x_k^2+y_k^2$, this is the Euclidean norm $\lVert\Phi(z)\rVert_2$ of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and it is a norm on
the real vector space underlying $\mathbb C^m$ in the sense of
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. Consequently
$\lVert z-w\rVert=\lVert\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\rVert_2$, so the metric of
$\mathbb C^m$, its balls ([[def-metric-ball]]), its open sets, its convergent
sequences, its Cauchy sequences and its continuous maps are **verbatim** those of
$\mathbb R^{2m}$ under $\Phi$. In particular convergence and continuity are
coordinatewise ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]), $\mathbb C^m$ is complete
([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]), and a subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

**At $m=1$ this is the published plane dictionary.** For $m=1$ the map $\Phi$ is
the bijection of [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]] and every clause
above reduces to a clause recorded there. Openness, connectedness and real total
differentiability on $\mathbb C^m$ are always read through $\Phi$, exactly as
that remark reads them through its own identification.

**What $\Phi$ does not carry.** $\Phi$ respects the additive and the real scalar
structure but not multiplication by $i$ in any way visible to a general
$\mathbb R$-linear map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$: an $\mathbb R$-linear map of
$\mathbb C^m$ need not be $\mathbb C$-linear. That distinction is the whole
content of the criterion the page proves next, and it is why "linear" is always
qualified below.

Let $m \ge 1$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}^m$ be a nonempty connected open set,
and let $f : U \to \mathbb{C}$ be holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). If there is a
nonempty open set $W \subseteq U$ such that $f(z) = 0$ for every $z \in W$, then
$f \equiv 0$ on $U$.

This is the several-variable identity theorem at the strength the page supports:
the hypothesis is a nonempty **open** set of zeros. An accumulation point of the
zero set is neither assumed nor sufficient in several variables; the companion
page records that stronger one-variable statement as false here.

Step 1.2 treats the case j=0 (empty product) explicitly as W_0 W_0^{-1}=I; the residual of step 2.1 is estimated from j=0 on.
n>=2 is assumed because the sequences of the cited lemma are stated for n>=2; the argument of steps 1.1-5.1 itself is dimension-free and no step uses more than the stated hypotheses.

The extra smallness CE_0<=1/16 of the statement is a non-strict hypothesis; step 1.2 uses it to keep the weighted product at most 1 and step 4.1 to keep the image inside the open domain, both with weak inequalities.

Step 3.1 lets j tend to infinity through the uniform convergence on L and step 4.1 extends the identity from the real slice to the strip; the closed strip boundary is never reached, since the identity is proved on the open strip.

The step constants may be enlarged and their smallness constant decreased, depending only on $n,	au$. Put $\Lambda:=\Omega_{\alpha,	au}$ and $W_j:=\operatorname{diag}(r_j^{-1}I_n,\sigma_j^{-1}I_n)$.

Let $H_0(z,
u)=e_0(
u)+
u\cdot I+P_0(z,
u)$ be holomorphic and real on real points on $D_{r_0,s_0,h_0}(\Lambda)$, with $|P_0|\le\varepsilon_0$. Suppose at every stage the cited one-step suppliers produce the following data:
